did_you_know.text: Did you know? In this chapter, Zophar the Naamathite responds to Job, thereby joining Job’s friends in their cycle of debates with him.

Did you know? Zophar argues that many words, rhetoric, and mockery do not prove that the speaker is right. In verses 2–4, he criticizes Job for presenting his words as pure and silencing his opponents.
Did you know? Zophar expresses the wish that God Himself would answer Job and reveal to him the “secrets of wisdom”—hidden wisdom that Job does not recognize.
Did you know? Through rhetorical questions, Zophar emphasizes that a person cannot fully investigate God or grasp the full depth of His wisdom.
Did you know? Zophar portrays God as the sovereign Lord whose actions no one can stop or call to account: if He imprisons or summons, no one can turn Him back.
Did you know? Zophar presents human beings as born lacking understanding and uses the image of a “wild donkey” to emphasize the need for learning, discipline, and growth.
Did you know? According to Zophar, the desired change begins with preparing the heart, raising one’s hands in prayer, and removing wrongdoing from one’s hands and household.
Did you know? Zophar connects turning away from wrongdoing with honor and security: a person will be able to hold his head high without shame, stand firm, and have no fear.
Did you know? Zophar promises that after making this change, a person will be able to leave his suffering behind, be renewed, and become bright like the morning.

Did you know? At the end of the chapter, a contrast is drawn between the hope and security promised to those who change their ways and the fate of the wicked, whose eyes will fail, whose escape will vanish, and whose hope will end in disappointment.
